unit-eng-t1-plot.title: Test 1 · 1 Plot Diagram
unit-eng-t1-plot.source: Test 1 notes · Plot Diagram (student’s own notes)

summary.text: The five parts of a plot diagram and the craft techniques that go with them, from your Test 1 notes: exposition (show don’t tell, integrate details, pace yourself), rising action and its three jobs, the climax, falling action and its two purposes, and the resolution.

why.text: Almost every question about a story’s structure reduces to naming which of five parts a moment belongs to. The one that actually costs marks is telling a tense rising-action beat from the climax, so that distinction gets the most room here.

objectives.text: Name all five parts of a plot diagram in order
Place a moment from an unfamiliar story into the right part
Tell the climax from a merely tense rising-action beat
Say what show-don’t-tell, integrate details and pace yourself each ask for
State the three jobs of rising action and the two purposes of falling action

parentNote.text: Built from Sedona’s own handwritten notes, so the definitions are her class’s, not ours. Two things worth knowing. Her notes’ examples stayed on the flashcards and every graded question uses a fresh story instead, so she cannot answer from memory of the page. And the distinction the questions push hardest — a tense beat is not automatically the climax, only the beat that TURNS the story is — is not stated that bluntly in the notes; it is the reliable way to answer the identification questions a test asks.

nextUp.text: Say the five parts out loud in order before you flip a single card.

cards.def:
**A graphic organizer that splits a story into five separate parts.**
• Exposition, rising action, climax, falling action, resolution.
• Drawn as a mountain — the climax is the peak.

**The foundation the story is built on.**
• Includes characters, setting and world-building.
• This is the “before” — the trouble has not taken hold yet.
cards.hint: Ex-position = the position everything starts from.

cards.def:
**Instead of SAYING a character is brave, SHOW them being brave.**
• A named trait is a claim; an action is evidence.
• An exposition technique.
cards.hint: A claim tells. A scene shows.

cards.def:
**Reveal information through dialogue, action or description.**
• The opposite is stopping the story to explain.
• This is about HOW the information arrives.

**Don’t explain everything at once — introduce details as they become necessary.**
• This is about WHEN the information arrives.
• Everything at once is a briefing, not a beginning.
cards.hint: As needed, not all at once.

cards.def:
**Sets the stage and is where the story begins to move forward.**
• Everything between the setup and the turning point.
cards.hint: The long climb up to the peak.

cards.def:
**Raises the stakes, starting from a small problem and growing it into a big one.**
• Small → large is the test: if the trouble never grows, it is not rising.
cards.hint: Small problem, bigger problem, biggest problem.

cards.def:
**True nature is revealed by what a character DOES.**
• Not by what the narrator calls them.

**Without compelling rising action, the climax feels unreal.**
• The turning point has to be EARNED by what came before it.
cards.hint: An unearned peak reads as unreal.

cards.def:
**The most intense or crucial part of the story — the turning point.**
• Only ONE moment turns the story; every other tense beat is rising action.
• Tense is not the test. Turning is the test.
cards.hint: The one beat the story cannot go back from.

cards.def:
**When the intense tension begins to dissipate and the story wraps up.**
• Starts the moment the turning point is behind you.
cards.hint: Coming down the far side of the mountain.

cards.term: The two purposes of falling action
cards.def:
**It lets the audience process the climax, and it transitions the story smoothly toward the conclusion.**
• Cut it and the ending arrives before the reader has caught up.

**The immediate consequences of what happened.**
• Does the setting change?
• How are the other characters reacting?
• It sets up the new normal.

**Ties up the significant threads.**
• Significant ones — not every thread in the book.
cards.hint: The knots that mattered get tied.

questions.q: Put these four moments from one story in the order a plot diagram would place them.
opts: Nadia is the only eighth grader on a robotics team that has never won a match
The team’s sensor fails at three straight practices and nobody will say whose code broke it
At the regional final Nadia tells the judges the bug was hers
The team keeps her on as lead programmer for next season
questions.hint: Which one could you read first and still understand nothing has gone wrong yet?
steps: The setup comes first: who she is and where she is, before any trouble.
Then the trouble grows — a fault nobody will own is a problem getting bigger.
The turning point is the moment she does the thing that changes everything.
What the team decides afterwards is the new normal, so it lands last.

ex.main: **Exposition, rising action, climax, resolution.** A plot diagram is a shape, and the shape is the order: set it up, wind it up, turn it, settle it.
ex.tip: When you are unsure which beat is the climax, ask which one the story could not undo.

questions.q: Which part of a plot diagram introduces the characters, the setting and the world, before the trouble has taken hold?
opts: Exposition
Rising action
Falling action
Resolution
questions.hint: It is the part the rest is built on top of.
steps: Ask what job the part does, not where it sits.
Characters, setting and world-building are all setup, not movement.
Setup is the foundation the story is built on.
That is the exposition.

ex.main: **Exposition.** It is named the foundation for a reason — it carries the weight of everything after it, and it is the only part where nothing has gone wrong yet.
ex.tip: Rising action can still introduce a character, but its job is to move the story, not to set it up.

questions.q: A novel has four scenes so tense you hold your breath. Only one of them changes the direction of the story for good. On a plot diagram, what are the other three?
opts: Climax
Rising action
Falling action
Exposition
questions.hint: How many turning points does one story get?
steps: A story has exactly one climax.
So three of those four tense scenes are not it.
Everything tense before the turning point is the climb toward it.
That climb is the rising action.

ex.main: **Rising action.** Being tense is not what makes a beat the climax — TURNING the story is. Three tense scenes that leave the story pointing the same way are the climb, not the peak.
ex.tip: This is the single commonest mix-up in the whole topic: intensity feels like a climax, but only one beat is one.

questions.q: A writer wants the reader to understand that Marcus is anxious. Which sentence SHOWS it rather than telling it?
opts: Marcus felt a familiar and quite overwhelming anxiety about the front door
Marcus was the most anxious person in his entire family
Marcus checked the lock, walked to the car, then came back and checked it again
Marcus had been an anxious child and was now an even more anxious adult
questions.hint: One of these would still work with the word “anxious” deleted from the language.
steps: Telling names the trait outright.
Showing gives you an action and lets you draw the conclusion.
Three of these hand you the word “anxious” and ask you to believe it.
Only the double-check at the lock makes you work it out — that is showing.

ex.main: **Checking the lock twice.** The reader concludes “anxious” for themselves, which is what makes it stick. A named trait is a claim; an action is evidence.
ex.tip: A quick test: cross out the trait word. If the sentence dies, it was telling.

questions.q: A writer needs the reader to learn that the narrator’s mother is a nurse. Which handling follows “integrate details”?
opts: Chapter Two: The Nurse
Her mother was a nurse at the county hospital and had been for eleven years
It is important to know that her mother worked in medicine
Her mother came in still wearing scrubs and asked who wanted the last orange
questions.hint: Integrating means the fact arrives while something else is happening.
steps: Integrating details means the information rides along on dialogue, action or description.
A sentence that stops to state a fact is the opposite of integrating it.
So is a narrator announcing what the reader should notice, or a chapter title doing the work.
The scrubs arrive inside a scene that was happening anyway.

ex.main: **The scrubs and the orange.** The fact is carried by an action the story wanted regardless, so nothing pauses to deliver it.
ex.tip: Integrate is about HOW a fact arrives. Pace yourself is about WHEN. Keep those two apart.

questions.q: Two writers each need the reader to learn the same ten facts about a town. Which choice follows “pace yourself”?
opts: Release each fact at the point the story first needs it
Put all ten in the opening chapter so nothing is confusing later
Hold all ten back for the final chapter as a surprise
Restate all ten at the start of every chapter
questions.hint: The rule is about timing, and its test is necessity.
steps: Pacing means introducing details as they become NECESSARY.
All ten up front is exactly the “everything at once” the rule warns against.
All ten at the end withholds what the story needed earlier, which is the same error reversed.
Releasing each fact where the story first needs it is the rule itself.

ex.main: **Release each fact where the story first needs it.** A reader remembers a detail they were given a reason to care about, and forgets one handed over before it mattered.
ex.tip: Front-loading feels thorough while you are writing it and reads as a lecture afterwards.

questions.q: In the middle of a novel, a disagreement over a borrowed bike grows until two families have stopped speaking. Which job of the rising action is that?
opts: Developing character
Building tension
Justifying the climax
Tying up threads
questions.hint: Look at the size of the problem at the start and at the end.
steps: Name what actually changed across the passage.
The problem itself got bigger: one bike, then two households.
Growing a small problem into a big one is the definition of building tension.
So this is tension-building.

ex.main: **Building tension.** The test is escalation — the stakes are higher at the end of the passage than at the start. A problem that stays the same size is not rising.
ex.tip: The three jobs do overlap in real stories. Ask which one the passage is MOSTLY doing.

questions.q: A reader finishes a novel and says the final confrontation felt like it came out of nowhere. Which job did the rising action most likely fail at?
opts: Introducing the setting and the world in the first chapter
Tying up the significant threads at the end of the book
Justifying the climax — the turning point was never built up to
Letting the reader process the confrontation afterwards
questions.hint: The complaint is about what was missing BEFORE the big moment.
steps: Locate the complaint in time: the reader is objecting to the climax feeling unearned.
Tying up threads and letting the reader process both happen after the climax, so neither is the cause.
Introducing the setting is exposition’s job, not the rising action’s.
That leaves the job of justifying the climax — building enough that the turn feels real.

ex.main: **Justifying the climax.** Your notes put it exactly: without compelling rising action, the climax feels unreal. “Out of nowhere” is a reader describing a peak that was never climbed to.
ex.tip: A climax is only as believable as the middle of the book makes it.

questions.q: The morning after the warehouse fire, neighbours stand in the road working out who will take which family in. Which part of the plot diagram is this?
opts: Exposition
Climax
Rising action
Falling action
questions.hint: The big event is over — this is the world reacting to it.
steps: Ask whether the intense moment is ahead or behind.
The fire has already happened, so the peak is behind us.
Working out who sleeps where shows the immediate consequences and starts a new normal.
Showing consequences and settling into a new normal is falling action.

ex.main: **Falling action.** It shows the immediate consequences, how other characters are reacting, and the shape of the new normal — all three of the things falling action is for.
ex.tip: Falling action is not filler. Without it the ending arrives before the reader has caught up.

questions.q: Which part of a plot diagram ties up the significant threads?
opts: Resolution
Falling action
Climax
Rising action
questions.hint: It is the last of the five.
steps: Work from the end backwards.
The final part of the diagram is where the story finishes its business.
Finishing that business is tying up the threads that mattered.
That is the resolution.

ex.main: **Resolution.** Note the word SIGNIFICANT — a resolution ties up the threads that mattered, not every thread the book ever started.
ex.tip: Falling action lowers the tension; the resolution closes the story out.

questions.q: Falling action has two primary purposes. Which pair names them?
opts: Introduce the remaining characters, and establish the rules of the world
Let the audience process the climax, and transition the story smoothly toward the conclusion
Raise the stakes steadily, and reveal each character’s true nature through what they do
State the theme outright, and tell the reader what to feel about it
questions.hint: Both purposes are about the reader, just after the biggest moment.
steps: Falling action sits between the peak and the ending, so its purposes face both ways.
Looking back: the reader needs a moment to take in what just happened.
Looking forward: the story has to get to its conclusion without lurching.
Processing and transitioning are the two.

ex.main: **Processing and transitioning.** Introducing the world is exposition and raising the stakes is rising action — both belong on the far side of the climax from this one.
ex.tip: If a film ends two seconds after the explosion, this is the part it skipped.

questions.q: Which detail belongs in the exposition of a story rather than anywhere else?
opts: The laundrette’s takings have gone missing three weeks running
The narrator finally tells her aunt what she overheard
The narrator lives above her aunt’s laundrette and has done since she was six
The narrator and her aunt reopen the shop together in the spring
questions.hint: Only one of these is true before anything goes wrong.
steps: Exposition is the setup: who, where, and the ordinary state of things.
A confrontation is a turning point and missing takings are trouble growing.
Reopening in the spring is a new normal, which comes after everything.
Living above the laundrette is the ordinary state of things.

ex.main: **Living above the laundrette.** It is a standing fact about her world, true before the story’s trouble starts — which is exactly what exposition carries.
ex.tip: Ask of any detail: could this be true on page one with nothing wrong yet?

questions.q: Why does the plot diagram call the exposition the “foundation” rather than just the beginning?
opts: Because a reader who skips it can still follow the plot perfectly well
Because it is always the longest section, and length is what makes it matter
Because it is the only part of the diagram allowed to contain description
Because everything later stands on it — stakes only matter if you know what is at risk
questions.hint: Think about what breaks later if the setup is thin.
steps: A foundation is about load, not order — it is what the rest rests on.
Length is not the point; plenty of stories open in a page.
Description turns up everywhere, so that cannot be it.
What makes it load-bearing is that stakes need something established to threaten.

ex.main: **Everything later stands on it.** You cannot raise the stakes for a reader who does not yet know what there is to lose — which is why a thin setup shows up as a flat middle.
ex.tip: Weak exposition rarely feels like an exposition problem. It feels like a boring rising action.

questions.q: A character everybody in the book describes as dependable is shown, over several chapters, quietly breaking three promises. Which job of the rising action is the writer leaning on hardest?
opts: Developing character — true nature is revealed by what they DO
Building tension — growing a small problem into a large one
Justifying the climax — earning the turning point in advance
Setting the scene — naming the time and place
questions.hint: Notice the gap between what people SAY about him and what he DOES.
steps: The passage sets a label against a pattern of actions.
Your notes are explicit: true nature is revealed by what a character does.
The actions here are contradicting the label everyone uses.
That is character development doing its job.

ex.main: **Developing character.** The writer has put a stated trait and a demonstrated one side by side, and the demonstrated one wins. That gap IS the characterisation.
ex.tip: When a label and an action disagree in a novel, believe the action.

questions.q: On the plot diagram drawn as a mountain, which part is the peak?
opts: The exposition
The climax
The falling action
The resolution
questions.hint: The shape is doing the explaining.
steps: The diagram climbs, peaks and descends.
The climb is the rising action and the descent is the falling action.
So the point where the climb becomes the descent is the peak.
That point is the climax.

ex.main: **The climax.** The picture is the definition: everything before it goes up, everything after it comes down, and the turn happens exactly once.
ex.tip: If you can draw the mountain you can usually reconstruct the five parts from it.

questions.q: A story shows, right after its turning point, that the corner shop has reopened under a new name and the neighbours now cross the road to avoid each other. What is that doing?
opts: Introducing the world and its people before any of the trouble starts
Building tension by growing one small problem into a much larger one
Showing the immediate consequences — the setting and the relationships both changed
Tying up every single thread the story has left open anywhere
questions.hint: Two things have changed, and the change is the point.
steps: Locate it: right after the turning point puts us in the falling action.
Falling action shows what the climax cost — has the setting changed, how are people reacting?
A renamed shop is a changed setting; crossing the road is a changed relationship.
So it is showing the immediate consequences.

ex.main: **Showing the immediate consequences.** Your notes list exactly these two questions — does the setting change, and how are other characters reacting — as what falling action puts on the page.
ex.tip: Consequences are how a reader learns the climax actually mattered.
